newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai bourse recovery seen resting on thin ice.
newsitem.headline: Thai bourse recovery seen resting on thin ice.

text.p: Thai stocks, which have rebounded after dipping near three-year lows earlier this month, could be hit again by political uncertainty and concerns over third-quarter corporate earnings, analysts said on Tuesday.

The analysts told Reuters investors were concerned about the political situation after Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa said on Saturday he would choose an appropiate successor and step down within seven days. His resignation was in exchange for support from coalition partners in a no-confidence vote.

The market initially rose on Banharn's resignation. But uncertainty over who would be the new premier and the ministers in charge of key economic portfolios were now major issues keeping investors from the market, analysts said.

"The index is likely to fall to between 960-1,000 points within the next two weeks if investors are not satisfied with the appointed prime minister and his cabinet. Investors want to see ministers who are capable of solving the economic problems," said Thanadech Mahapokai, first assistant vice president of Book Club Finance and Securities.
The market ended up 7.84 points on Tuesday at 1042.21.

"The index isn't expected to rise as long as investors are not sure whether the new cabinet could solve economic problems," said Suleeyaporn Tasanasrit, associate sales director of UBS (East Asia) Securities.

The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index slid to 982.03 points on September 10, below the key psychological level of 1,000. It was the lowest close since September 30, 1993 when the index ended at 971.44.

The drop was attributed to a lack of investor confidence in the government's ability to handle the country's slowing economy, rising trade deficits and sagging exports. Analysts said forced sales by investors unable to meet margin calls further depressed the market.

Under forced selling, investors are required to put up money for their stocks if prices drop below 40 percent of the purchase value of the stocks. If investors cannot find funds, they will be ordered by their brokers to sell the shares.

Two market support funds set up by the government and private sector helped boost the volatile index. The funds, which would provide up to 25.7 billion baht ($1.03 billion), were established to buy stocks and lend money to investors facing the prospect of having to force-sell shares to pay off debts.
Suleeyaporn said so far only about two billion baht ($80 million) of a 15.7 billion baht support fund set up by bankers and brokers has been invested in the market.
Analysts said investment from the baht fund concentrated mainly on buying blue-chip stocks, which was why the fund was not active despite entering the market nearly three weeks ago.
Apart from political concerns, investors were also worried about third-quarter corporate earnings.
"Investors have high expectations that earning growth of banks and finance firms during the third quarter would fall from earlier anticipation," Thanadech said.
Thanadech said his company recently revised profit growth for the banking sector, which is heavily weighted in the SET, to five percent in 1996 from the 15-18 percent forecast earlier.
"The revision was made because of a decline in banks' credit extension, a narrowing in banks' spreads and an increase in cash reserves to cover suspected bad debts," Thanadech said. ($1.00=25 baht)
